article_title: Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993.
citation: United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris (France). Environmental Education Section. (1993). Connect: UNESCO-UNEP Environmental Education Newsletter, 1993. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED368567
title: Goal-oriented framework sequencing EE instructional strategies from ecological foundations through conceptual awareness and investigation skills to environment action skills
description: The newsletter proposes a goal-oriented framework as a basis for organizing instructional strategies for global change education, matching activity types to goal levels. "Agoal-oriented frameworkcould also be used as a basis for organizing instructional strategies." Simulations, models and reading lay the ecological foundations; case-histories, field trips, brainstorming and discussions build conceptual awareness; secondary source investigations, primary data collection, value clarification and moral education develop investigation skills and evaluation of issues; and action workshops, community internship and action analysis projects build environment action skills.
requirements: Instruction must be organized so that activity types match the goal level being targeted, from ecological foundations up to environment action skills
target_learners: school students in global change / environmental education programmes
examples: The article lists simulations, models and reading for ecological foundations; case-histories, field trips, brainstorming sessions and discussions for conceptual awareness; and action workshops, action learning in community internship and action analysis projects for environment action skills

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Token reward with mapped milestone prizes sustaining engagement across tutoring sessions
description: Pirate Math embeds a motivational routine in its tutoring sessions: students receive gold coins for good work and place them on a treasure map. When they reach a picture of a treasure box, they earn a small prize. This recurring reward cycle structures motivation across the 16-week program.
requirements: A treasure map and small prizes must be available across the 16-week session sequence
target_learners: Third graders in remedial math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and effort in tutoring sessions
examples: Students receive gold coins for good work, place them on a treasure map, and earn a small prize on reaching the treasure box picture.

article_title: Strengthening the Educator Pipeline through Service Scholarships: California's Golden State Teacher Grant Program
citation: Leung-Gagné, M., Maria Castillo, M., Patrick, S. K., Carver-Thomas, D., Kini, T., Bingener, C., & Giani, M. V. (2025). Strengthening the educator pipeline through service scholarships: California's Golden State Teacher Grant Program. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/518.478
title: California Golden State Teacher Grant (GSTG) Program
description: A California service scholarship administered by the California Student Aid Commission that provides teacher candidates and Pupil Personnel Services candidates "an upfront grant as part of their overall student aid package to offset a substantial portion of their cost of preparation." In exchange, recipients commit to teach in a priority school or California State Preschool Program for 2 years, repaying the grant (prorated for partial completion) if they do not. The program has provided over $570 million since 2020–21 and its parameters—award amount, eligibility, service length—have changed repeatedly as funding varied.
requirements: Recipients must be enrolled in an approved, California-based preliminary teaching or PPS credential program through a student teaching or residency pathway and commit to serve in a priority school, where at least 55% of enrolled students are eligible for free or reduced-price meals, are English learners, or are living in foster care
constraints: The maximum award was reduced from $20,000 to $10,000 in July 2024, interns were excluded from eligibility, and lower-income applicants are prioritized when funds run short
target_learners: Pupil Personnel Services credential candidates (school counselors, social workers, psychologists)
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining a well-prepared, diverse educator workforce for high-need schools and shortage subjects
examples: In 2023–24, 45% of California's new teacher candidates received a GSTG; over the first 5 years the program supported 22,851 teacher candidates and 5,812 PPS candidates

article_title: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom
citation: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7
title: Goldin's engagement structures framework: affect as a representational system integral to mathematical engagement
description: The study draws on DeBellis and Goldin's and Goldin's framework in which affect operates as a representational system alongside cognition during mathematical work. Central to this perspective is the notion of engagement structures, defined in the article as "recurrent yet dynamically evolving conﬁgurations of affect, motiva- tion, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reason- ing" that shape participation in problem-solving. Each structure is organized around a motivating desire (e.g., Get the Job Done, Help Me, I'm Really into This), and contexts can produce branching, replacement, or stabilization of structures. The article extends the framework to classrooms where AI-generated emotional alerts become elements of the situation that may interact with students' affective pathways.
requirements: Requires analyzing affect, motivation, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reasoning together during in-the-moment mathematical activity rather than as separate predictors or outcomes.
constraints: The article states that constructs such as affective representations, affective pathways, motivating desires, and engagement structures are theoretically informed analytic interpretations rather than directly observable emotional states.
target_learners: high school mathematics students during problem-solving
target_learning_goals: integration of affect with mathematical reasoning
examples: The author coded episodes for engagement processes of activation, stabilization, and branching, and for teacher responses including reframing, reinforcement, collective discussion, inquiry, and non-intervention.
key_sources: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7

article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: Three-property schema for usable writing feedback: goal-orientation, anchoring, and prioritization
description: The article operationalizes three properties that writing research identifies as making feedback usable for revision: goal-orientation (engaging the rhetorical goal the writer is pursuing), anchoring (pointing to the specific text where revision should occur), and prioritization (ranking the most important revisions). The article states these address distinct revision needs: "what, where, and in what order", and that feedback usable for revision requires all three. In FOXGLOVE every feedback giver produces sentence-level comments labeled with one of five argumentative goals (Position, Claim, Evidence, Counterclaim, Rebuttal), anchors them to contiguous sentences, and ranks the three most urgent comments.
requirements: Feedback must be anchored to one or more contiguous full sentences, address exactly one goal per comment, and include an urgency ranking and a global comment
constraints: The schema encodes one particular view of what good feedback is and is intended as one lens on feedback quality, not a definitive standard
examples: Instructors and LLMs both produced feedback under this schema, enabling systematic comparison of where human and model feedback align and diverge
key_sources: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Six-dimension governance profile framework for characterizing AI teaching tools
description: A governance profile is "an explicit account of how an AI-mediated teaching tool distributes pedagogical authority, learner agency, human accountability, contextual boundaries, and evaluation visibility". The framework comprises six dimensions: pedagogical grounding, AI instructional authority, human accountability and control, learner agency and cognitive engagement, context specificity and boundary setting, and evaluation visibility and revision. Each dimension carries a core design question, typical mechanisms, and evidence of fit, avoiding collapse of governance into a single strict-to-permissive continuum.
requirements: Dimensions are analytically separable but interact in practice; profiles must be matched to the tool's instructional function
constraints: Constructed abductively from seven institutional tools and tested on four published systems; not intended as an exhaustive taxonomy of AI tools in computing education
target_learning_goals: designing, comparing, and evaluating AI-mediated learning environments
examples: Table 1 maps each dimension to mechanisms such as instructor-authored rubrics, staff approval gates, reflection prompts, and prompt and content versioning
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Match the governance profile to the instructional function (governance fit)
description: The article argues that "responsible scale in genAI-supported computing education depends on governance fit: coherence between the instructional function of a tool and the governance mechanisms in its design". Tools performing different functions — drafting official forum replies, simulating students for GTA rehearsal, prompting reflection, critiquing code style — should not share one interaction pattern, because each assigns different authority to the AI, responsibility to humans, and intellectual work to learners.
requirements: Designers must specify the instructional function of a tool before selecting governance mechanisms such as rubrics, approval gates, or reflection schemas
constraints: The goal is not a universal permission policy for genAI in computing courses
target_learning_goals: aligning AI tool design with intended learning processes
examples: BoilerTAI's approval gate is described as "the core workflow" for official course communication, while Owlgorithm is governed through learner reflection rather than answer delivery
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance carried by instructional artifacts that predate the AI system
description: A recurring cross-case pattern in which "governance is often carried by instructional artifacts that predate the AI system: rubrics, learning objectives, scenario banks, style guides, or content development workflows". These artifacts encode local values into the tool and provide a stable reference for evaluating outputs that would otherwise be judged only by surface plausibility. GLOW (rubric anchoring), Owlgorithm (reflection schema), CodeStylist (course style guide), and GAIDE (reproducible workflow) instantiate this pattern.
requirements: Local artifacts such as rubrics or style guides must exist and be encoded into the tool's constraints
constraints: Artifacts must be maintained as course materials change
examples: GLOW constrains AI-simulated student personas with an office-hour conversation rubric interpreted through programmatic coaching
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance enacted by workflow placement, with human-in-the-loop specified as a concrete workflow relation
description: A second cross-case pattern in which governance is enacted by placing the AI at a specific point in the instructional workflow. BoilerTAI gives the AI authority to draft forum responses while staff approve what becomes visible; BoilerSketch places TA supervision around diagram generation because diagrams "can appear authoritative even when they encode a subtle misconception". The article stresses that "human in the loop" is most useful when specified as a concrete workflow relation, since configuring, vetting, editing, approving, interpreting, and coaching are different forms of control.
requirements: A specific workflow point must exist where human review or approval can be inserted before outputs reach students
constraints: Supervision is described as especially appropriate for routine topics where staff can rapidly inspect generated representations
examples: BoilerTAI addresses forum response scaling while preserving staff accountability for the final instructional message
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance through learner role design: preserving student intellectual work via critique, reflection, debugging, and revision
description: A third cross-case pattern in which governance operates through the learner role the tool constructs. AI-Lab, Owlgorithm, and CodeStylist preserve meaningful student work by shaping AI use around critique, reflection, debugging, and revision. The article states that "learner agency is not abstract; it is an interaction pattern that can be designed" — for example, Owlgorithm prompts explanation after accepted submissions and debugging after failed ones, while CodeStylist positions AI feedback as an invitation to revise.
requirements: The interaction must leave the central learning work — reasoning, debugging, revision decisions — with the student
examples: AI-Lab expects students to interrogate AI output rather than merely consume it, developing judgment about when AI output is useful or misleading
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance strengthened through visibility and revision: each profile points to the evidence that matters for it
description: A fourth cross-case pattern: "governance becomes stronger when it is visible to instructors and revisable". Rubric-domain analytics, edit and approval traces, student ratings, survey and focus-group evidence, and staff review make tool behavior inspectable and allow revision of rubrics, prompts, scenarios, and approval practices. Because each tool performs a different instructional function, a single portfolio cannot be evaluated through one common outcome measure; instead each governance profile links design choices to evaluation choices.
requirements: Logs, dashboards, edit traces, or ratings must be collected and interpreted by course staff
constraints: Evidence of fit differs by profile — e.g., rubric alignment for rubric-governed tools, edit traces and staff workload for approval-gate tools
examples: For BoilerTAI, relevant evidence includes response timeliness, final answer quality, staff edit effort, and student satisfaction
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students' ChatGPT Use for Learning
citation: Øby, E. (2026). Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students’ ChatGPT Use for Learning. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5apqd333
title: Goal orientation theory perspective on students' motivational orientations toward generative AI use
description: Goal orientation theory is the article's second foundational lens, supplying the motivational component of the framework. The abstract reports that the synthesis draws "on cognitive load theory and goal orientation theory" and that "motivational orientations" are among the mechanisms that "may shape students’ decisions about when and how to rely on generative AI tools during academic work". It thus links students' goals to scaffold-versus-shortcut patterns of AI use.
requirements: Combination with cognitive load theory and the mediating constructs within the integrative framework
constraints: Conceptual treatment; motivational orientations are proposed influences, not measured variables
target_learning_goals: Orientation toward learning rather than task completion when using AI

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Goal-by-Environment framework for classifying simulated student systems
description: The article proposes organizing the simulated-student design space along two dimensions: behavioral goals (performance, learning, human aspects) and environment (subject domain, learner population, interaction modality). Its purpose is comparability: "two systems can both be called “simulated students” yet be incommensurate", so making the dimensions explicit prevents overclaiming and aligns evaluation with the fidelity notion actually claimed for a given setting.
requirements: A system must declare which behavioral goal it targets and in which environment it is deployed for its evaluation to be interpretable
constraints: Simulators built for different goals and environments are not directly comparable to one another
target_learners: Researchers and developers of LLM-based educational simulation systems
target_learning_goals: Educational validity and comparability of simulated-learner evaluations
examples: Table 1 maps the four applied contexts (teacher training, social learning, data generation, content evaluation) onto behavioral goals and environmental considerations
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Evaluate simulated students on goal-aligned fidelity rather than surface realism
description: The article recommends that evaluation prioritize whether simulated behavior matches the simulator's declared behavioral goal and environment, not fluency or generic humanness. "Evaluation should prioritize goal-aligned fidelity rather than surface realism", because fluent dialogue can mask implausible learning dynamics, and simulators built for different purposes require fundamentally different success criteria. Metrics should be derived from the goal: error distributions for performance settings, trajectory metrics for learning settings, interactional metrics for human-aspects settings.
requirements: Metrics must be derived from the simulator's behavioral goal and deployment environment; learning-oriented settings require trajectory metrics such as gradual improvement and sensitivity to feedback
constraints: The fidelity-evaluation gap arises when fluent dialogue and generic humanness scores are taken as evidence of educational validity
target_learners: Researchers and evaluators of simulated student systems
target_learning_goals: Valid, non-overclaimed evaluation of simulated learner fidelity
examples: The article specifies that performance and data-generation settings call for controlled error distributions and resistance to drifting into expert reasoning
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Explaining learning engagement in AI-assisted learning through teacher support and achievement goals: insights from goal-setting theory
citation: Yongliang Wang & Yaobo Wang. (2026). Explaining learning engagement in AI-assisted learning through teacher support and achievement goals: insights from goal-setting theory. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 13:1215. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-07636-8
title: Goal-setting Theory extended to AI-assisted learning: approach-oriented goals as the primary motivational pathways from external support to engagement
description: Goal-setting Theory, articulated by Locke and refined by Locke and Latham, holds that consciously set goals regulate action, with specific, challenging, attainable goals directing attention, energizing effort, sustaining persistence, and fostering strategy development. The study integrates teacher support, the 2×2 achievement goal framework, and engagement into a single structural model and argues that in AI-assisted environments, where "immediate feedback and visible progress indicators" make goal pursuit more salient and self-regulated, approach-oriented goals become the primary pathways translating external support into engagement, while avoidance goals do not function as effective conduits.
requirements: Learners must be operating in AI-assisted learning environments characterized by immediate feedback and visible progress indicators for the context-sensitive extension to apply
constraints: The extension is grounded in cross-sectional self-report data, which the authors state prevents causal inferences
target_learners: Chinese university EFL students with prior AI-assisted learning experience
target_learning_goals: English language learning engagement and motivation in AI-assisted contexts
examples: The study tested a hypothesized model (Fig. 1) linking teacher support, four achievement goal orientations, and engagement with SEM in a sample of 758 learners
key_sources: Yongliang Wang & Yaobo Wang. (2026). Explaining learning engagement in AI-assisted learning through teacher support and achievement goals: insights from goal-setting theory. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 13:1215. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-07636-8

article_title: Using chatbots to support student goal setting and social presence in fully online activities: learner engagement and perceptions
citation: Hew, K. F., Huang, W., Du, J., & Jia, C. (2023). Using chatbots to support student goal setting and social presence in fully online activities: learner engagement and perceptions. Journal of Computing in Higher Education, 35, 40–68. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-022-09338-x
title: Goal-setting chatbot using five SMART-framework questions before online class
description: A chatbot used in Study 1 to support student goal setting in a fully online course. Prior to attending class, participants completed a goal-setting activity with the chatbot, which “engaged participants with five questions developed based on the SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and timely) goal setting framework”. The chatbot served as a pre-class self-regulation prompt for online learners.
requirements: Learners must complete the goal-setting activity with the chatbot prior to attending the online class session.
target_learners: higher education students in fully online courses
target_learning_goals: goal setting and self-regulated learning for online class activities
examples: Study 1 participants in a fully online course completed the chatbot-led goal setting activity before class.

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: GOMS analysis approach
description: GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules) analysis, developed by Card, Moran, and Newell (1983), models human-computer interaction as an executable model built from goal hierarchies, operator sequences (methods), and selection rules for choosing among methods. The report states "a GOMS analysis models human-computer interaction as relatively domain-independent procedural skills." Data come from videotaped behavior and time-stamped keystroke files coded into operator-sequence protocols, yielding timing information for component goals.
requirements: Empirically derived estimates of user processing speed, short-term memory capacity and duration, and other cognitive parameters, plus protocol data from users performing the task
constraints: System knowledge of how the computer works and domain knowledge are assumed irrelevant and not modeled; the approach was developed for computer tasks rather than knowledge-rich problem solving
target_learners: Computer users performing text-editing and similar interface tasks
target_learning_goals: Efficient execution of procedural human-computer interaction methods
examples: The report reproduces a GOMS model of a text-editing task with goals such as Insert and Delete, operators such as Scroll-to and Type, and selection rules such as the Top 2/3 rule

article_title: Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory
citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Goal representation as a common component linking executive functions, with mixing costs indexing it and local costs indexing switch implementation
description: The article adopts the task-switching framework in which flexibility has two components: goal representation (monitoring for the need to switch and selecting the relevant task goal), indexed by mixing costs, and switch implementation (the actual switch to the newly relevant task-set), indexed by local costs. Mixing costs "mainly reflect the additional necessity of generating/abstracting the relevant task goal," whereas local costs are "viewed as primarily sensitive to difficulties in switch implementation." The authors use this decomposition to test whether inhibition and working memory differentially support the two components, and conclude the executive-skill relation to flexibility "seems exclusively driven by goal representation."
requirements: Task batteries must include both baseline and mixed-task blocks, as in the Shape School, to compute mixing and local costs separately
constraints: Costs are meaningful only for participants with rudimentary switching abilities; perseveration must be modeled to avoid artificial distortion of cost magnitudes
target_learning_goals: understanding the executive-control processes supporting cognitive flexibility in early childhood
examples: The study computed mixing costs as baseline versus no-shift trial contrasts and local costs as no-shift versus shift trial contrasts within the Shape School switch condition
key_sources: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Goal maintenance account of preschoolers' poor working memory performance
description: The article proposes that preschoolers' poor working memory performance may partly reflect goal neglect: when the representation of the task goal (maintaining items for recall) is not sufficiently active amid competing goals, recall suffers. Working memory tasks involve switching between encoding, concurrent-task, maintenance and recall goals, so "memory performance can, at least in part, depend on the efficiency of goals maintenance". Transparent cues and goal-oriented motor activity are proposed as supports for keeping the goal active during the retention interval.
requirements: The task must involve competing goals between encoding, a concurrent activity, and recall, so that goal maintenance is required
constraints: The authors note the alternative hypothesis that finger tracking is too demanding for younger children must be eliminated before final conclusions about the strategy-based interpretation
target_learning_goals: maintaining task-relevant information in working memory across a retention interval
examples: The study operationalized goal support as a school-bag cue that carried the memory items to the recall point, tracked visually or with a finger during the retention interval
key_sources: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4

article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Embed goal-oriented motor activity on a transparent goal cue to scaffold young children's memory for instructions
description: The article recommends that educational settings integrate motor, goal-oriented activity to scaffold memory in young children. A transparent goal cue improves working memory performance only when children act on it continuously — "proposing a goal-oriented gesture on the cue is crucial to boost recall performance". The cue should make the task goal transparent (e.g., a school bag carrying the to-be-recalled items to the recall point) and remain present during the full retention interval.
requirements: A transparent goal cue that remains present during the full retention interval
A motor activity oriented toward the goal that children perform continuously on the cue
constraints: The benefit was shown in 5-year-olds but not in 4-year-olds, for whom the supplementary instructions and fine motor tracking demands may have overloaded attention
target_learning_goals: remembering instructions or items across a delay
maintaining the task goal during a retention interval
examples: In the experiment, 5-year-olds finger-tracked a school-bag cue that transported the memory items to the recall point during a 7,100 ms retention interval, improving recall relative to the abstract cue

title: Google's Computational Thinking for Educators free online course with community of practice
description: Google provides "a free online course called Computational Thinking for Educators" structured around algorithms and patterns for four groups of teachers: humanities, mathematics, science, and computer science teachers. Beyond online materials, it offers "a community of practice that provides a place for educators to share ideas, challenges, solutions, and resources learned from their classroom practice." The article presents it as an accessible starting point for teachers interested in embedding CT.

target_learning_goals: teachers' computational thinking understanding and pedagogical approaches to embedding CT
examples: The article directs teachers interested in learning more to Google's course as a good place to start and connect with a community of teachers

article_title: The richness of CSCL environments

description: The article identifies Dykman's (1998) goal-orientation model of depression vulnerability as "the most influential model of achievement goals and internalizing problems." It postulates that "achievement goals lead to specific cognitive sets and appraisal patterns that have important implications for people's mental health": mastery-focused individuals perceive negative outcomes as growth opportunities and show lower depressive symptoms, while performance-focused individuals tie self-worth to social comparison and are more vulnerable to depression. The article extends the model to anxiety and to the approach-avoidance distinction.

constraints: The article notes the relation between achievement goals and internalizing problems is posited to be reciprocal, so the model is not strictly unidirectional.

description: The article applies Koriat et al.'s distinction to CLT self-report items: effort phrased as personal investment captures "goal-driven effort", which "relies on top-down processing, reflecting voluntary decisions made by learners", whereas effort phrased as task demand captures "data-driven effort", based on bottom-up task characteristics the learner cannot control, similar to difficulty. The study operationalized these as two distinct appraisal conditions and tested their differential relationships with response time and accuracy.

title: Goal congruity theory: role attitudes depend on congruity between a role's communal/agentic goal affordances and personally valued goals
description: Goal congruity theory, rooted in expectancy-value theory, holds that attitudes toward a social role such as being a scientist are shaped by the goal affordances the role offers and how well those affordances match personally endorsed goals. The article states that "Goal congruity theory posits that individuals' attitudes towards a social role (e.g., being a scientist) are influenced by the communal/agentic goal affordances associated with that role and the congruity between those affordances and personally valued goals." Communal goals concern collaboration and helping others; agentic goals concern advancement and recognition. The study extends the theory to Indigenous STEM populations longitudinally, with belonging as a mediating mechanism.
requirements: Measurement of both perceived goal affordances in the role and personal goal endorsement, operationalized here via POMP-converted difference scores for incongruity
constraints: The article notes most prior goal congruity research used White middle-class samples, limiting generalizability, and that evidence for incongruity effects has been inconsistent across communal and agentic goals

target_learning_goals: sense of belonging in STEM disciplines
examples: The study measured four communal goals (including serving community and nation-building) and three agentic goals (recognition, success, independence) across three survey waves over 12 months

citation: Kate Gordon. (1916). A Class Experiment with the Hillegas Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducpsych
title: Gordon's reconciliation account: the scale steadies judgment of a single composition but does not alter relative judgments of a series
description: Gordon proposes that the scale's effect is to reduce inconsistency in marking any one composition, while leaving each judge's and the group's ordering of the compositions relatively intact. She writes that "whereas the scale does steady the judgment of a group with respect to its marking of a single composition, it does not alter the judgment... with respect to the relative merits of a series of compositions." This accounts for the coexistence of reduced ranges and standard deviations with unchanged correlations.

constraints: Inferred from one class experiment with forty-one inexperienced judges and twenty-five freshman compositions; the author frames it as her interpretation of seemingly conflicting results

citation: Tsuda, A., Manalo, E., Teramae, T., & Noda, T. (2026). Unveiling the Impact of Goal Types: Enhancing Self-Efficacy in Rehabilitation Robotics. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00444-4
title: Four goal structures (process, outcome, shift, transform) adapted from Zimmerman's framework for robot-assisted motor learning
description: The study adapts Zimmerman and colleagues' goal-type framework into four manipulated conditions for exoskeleton-assisted practice. In the robot context, "outcome-goal participants focused on achieving the highest score and verbally reported their scores after each throw," process-goal participants concentrated on executing key movement components, transform-goal participants monitored outcomes and reported adjustments, and shift-goal participants began with movement execution before shifting to performance outcomes. The framework assumes skill acquisition proceeds through phases, with outcome goals suited to later, procedurally stable stages.

constraints: Derived from non-clinical, healthy, novice learners in a single session; generalizability of the stage-based ordering to clinical rehabilitation populations is untested

examples: The experiment assigned 100 participants to the four goal conditions or a practice-only control during 15 minutes of robot-assisted boccia practice

citation: Angela D. Bender, Hannah L. Filmer, Claire K. Naughtin and Paul E. Dux. (2017). Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-speciﬁc improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0015-4
title: Cognitive training interventions should include active controls, randomization, theory-targeted outcomes, and related transfer tasks
description: Drawing on recent reviews of cognitive training, the article states that "a gold standard cognitive intervention should (1) employ outcome measures with a clear targeted theoretical construct; (2) minimize potential placebo effects... by including an active control group", (3) randomize participants, and (4) restrict transfer tasks to theoretically related ones. The study applied these by using a single-task active control, randomization, and a factor-analytically grounded transfer battery.

Random allocation of participants to treatment or control
Outcome measures with a clear targeted theoretical construct
Transfer tasks restricted to tasks related to the trained construct
constraints: A no-contact control group was deliberately not included because such groups often differ in motivation and expectancy effects

article_title: Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions
citation: Yajing Zhang, Thi Kim Truc Huynh and Benjamin James Dyson. (2023). Deliberately making miskates: Behavioural consistency under win maximization and loss maximization conditions. npj Science of Learning 8:55. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00206-6
title: Goal-incongruent feedback account of performance disruption after wins and losses
description: The article proposes that the disruptive effect of negative feedback is not inherent to its valence but arises from a mismatch between feedback and the learner's current goal, termed goal-incongruent feedback. Drawing on consistency theory and goal-directed learning, it argues that "the traditional disruption generated by losses is the result of incongruity with the goal (implicit or explicit) of win maximization", and that wins disrupt behaviour equivalently when the goal is losing. Learners can thus flexibly redefine 'success'. The account reframes loss-related performance costs as goal-state mismatches rather than intrinsic properties of negative outcomes.
requirements: The learner's goal (win or loss maximization) must be established, implicitly or explicitly, so feedback can be evaluated as congruent or incongruent with it.
constraints: The study used abstracted points-based feedback with the visually presented words 'win' and 'lose'; the authors note that "the use of points system represents abstracted rather than concrete forms of feedback" and question whether consistency remains isomorphic with more tangible rewards and punishments.
target_learners: Adult participants in competitive decision-making games (university students)
target_learning_goals: Flexible interpretation of performance feedback; adaptive goal-directed adjustment of outcome-action strategies
examples: Participants instructed to "Just try to do as BADLY as you can! Try to get the most negative score." showed behavioural disruption following wins, mirroring disruption following losses under win maximization.

citation: Alexandra O. Cohen, Kate Nussenbaum, Hayley M. Dorfman, Samuel J. Gershman and Catherine A. Hartley. (2020). The rational use of causal inference to guide reinforcement learning strengthens with age. npj Science of Learning 5:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00075-3
title: Three-territory gold-mining reinforcement learning task with hidden agents
description: A developmental adaptation of the Dorfman et al. task in which participants choose between two mines with fixed reward probabilities (80% vs 20% gold) across three 50-trial blocks. Each block occurs in a territory visited by a hidden agent that intervenes on 30% of trials: a Millionaire who adds gold, a Robber who replaces gold with rocks, or a Sheriff who intervenes randomly. After each outcome participants report whether the agent caused it. The task measures learning via optimal choice and causal attribution via forced judgments, supporting computational model comparison across ages.

constraints: The exact intervention probability (30%) was not told to participants; intervention was invisible and ambiguous on each trial.

examples: Ninety participants (ages 7–25, M age = 15.89) completed three blocks of 50 trials; 12 additional participants were excluded for selecting the better option on fewer than 60% of trials.

article_title: Reflections on Andes’ Goal-free User Interface
citation: VanLehn, K. (2015). Reflections on Andes' Goal-free User Interface. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0067-7
title: Goal-free vs. goal-aligned user interfaces for step-based tutoring systems
description: A goal-aligned user interface displays relevant goals as blank boxes or constrained entry locations that scaffold problem-solving steps; a goal-free user interface is "essentially a blank canvas, with no visual indications of the goals that should be attempted next". Andes implemented the goal-free vision so users could enter steps anywhere and in any order, like paper, while the system still recognized goals and correctness. The design requires the system to do plan recognition, interpret composite steps, and support assessment without location-based goal cues.
requirements: The tutoring system must provide goal scaffolding on demand via next-step and what's-wrong hint buttons
The system must decompose large composite steps into primitive physics rules
Immediate feedback keeps students on a recognizable solution path
constraints: Plan recognition works poorly because users often have no recognizable plan
Embedded assessment (assignment of blame) is much harder because an incorrect step's location provides no information about the user's intended goal
examples: Andes3, released around 2010, looked and acted like MS PowerPoint, with tools for text, equations, arrows and coordinate axes, and offered text auto-completions when defining variables

title: GoSaveThem VR mass casualty incident triage simulation
description: GoSaveThem is a VR software with mass casualty incident scenarios, selected because it was "the only known available application adjusted to Swedish conditions." Participants use a fully immersive HTC VIVE head-mounted display to walk through a post-explosion subway station scene with 22 victim avatars, performing primary triage. Handheld controllers with vibrations simulate assessing a pulse, and breathing sounds play near an avatar's chest, enabling realistic respiratory rate assessments and actions like applying tourniquets and assigning triage colors.
requirements: A fully immersive head-mounted display and handheld controllers; participants need 5–15 minutes of familiarization with the VR technique before the research scenario
constraints: Technical and contextual conclusions are related to this specific VR system and setup; caution should be taken before generalizing to other VR platforms
target_learning_goals: primary triage in mass casualty incidents
examples: Participants triaged victims in a scenario of an explosion in a subway station, ending when they evacuated after finding explosives, completed triage, or after approximately 20 minutes

title: Set clear career goals in student skills education because goal-setting may be associated with faster skill acquisition
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that making goals clear in student education may support skill acquisition: "As demonstrated in this study, goal-setting in student education may be associated with skill acquisition". In the study, students who aspired to become surgeons improved at a significantly faster rate than peers with other aspirations despite comparable baselines. The influence of the awarding of study credits on feedback use and test-taking motivation in medical progress testing. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10324-4
title: Goal orientation theory: performance-oriented versus learning-oriented students respond differently to formative testing
description: The article invokes goal orientation theory, which "states that the individual goal orientation affects motivation, which in turn guides behavioural responses". Performance-oriented students valued the summative PT as more important because of its consequences for study credits, put less effort into the formative PT, and were less motivated to consult its feedback; learning-oriented students valued PT feedback for self-assessment and self-study regardless of assessment condition. A contextual factor, temporariness (future summative testing), encouraged some learning-oriented students to take formative PTs seriously.
requirements: Distinguishing students' orientations relies on qualitative interview data rather than explicitly stated goals
constraints: Students did not explicitly state goals for the PT; they showed a more general focus on either learning or performance
target_learners: second- and third-year bachelor medical students
examples: Performance-oriented students reported guessing or looking up answers during the formative test; learning-oriented students used the formative test as self-assessment or as a self-study tool generating instant feedback

title: Two-part flipped classroom module with online pre-class materials and in-class case-based activities
description: The intervention was a two-part pharmacology module. The first part was "self-study through an online 'Google group' where study aids, topic introductions, and prerecorded videos were posted a week before the class". The second part consisted of in-class activities: an MCQ pretest, subgroup discussions of 5–6 students, projected case scenarios, facilitator supplementation, and a post-test, with an end-of-module essay test 15 days after sessions. It was compared against conventional instructor-led tutorials in the quasi-experiment.

active participation and application of knowledge in class
examples: Study aids, topic introductions, and prerecorded videos were posted to a Google group one week before each class; sessions used case scenarios discussed in subgroups of 5–6 students with pre- and post-tests each session

title: Godin's integrated behavior change framework for health professionals: intention, shaped by four modifiable psychosocial factors, drives health-professional behavior
description: Godin's integrated behavior change framework, informed by the Theory of Planned Behavior and a systematic review of 76 studies, assumes that intention influences the behavior of health professionals. Intention is in turn shaped by physician characteristics and "four modifiable psychosocial factors: beliefs about capabilities, moral norm, social influences and beliefs about consequences". This study used the framework to structure its quantitative analysis of CPD course impact, measuring each construct with CPD-REACTION and testing which factors predicted post-course intention.
requirements: Measurement of intention and its psychosocial determinants with a validated instrument such as CPD-REACTION, adapted to the targeted behavior
constraints: The framework itself assumes intention influences behavior, and the article notes high intention scores do not necessarily ensure actual behavior change; moderate to high intention is generally linked to modest to moderate behavior change
target_learning_goals: adoption of targeted clinical practice behaviors after CPD
examples: The study operationalized the framework's four psychosocial factors with CPD-REACTION items (beliefs about capabilities three items, social influences three items, moral norm two items, beliefs about consequences two items) across nine CPD courses.

citation: Fisher H, Zabar S, Chodosh J, Langford A, Trinh-Shevrin C, Sherman S, Altshuler L. (2022). A novel simulation-based approach to training for recruitment of older adults to clinical trials. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-022-01643-4
title: Virtual three-station GOSCE with standardized participants and an 11-item behaviorally anchored communication checklist
description: The GOSCE is a "more cost-and resource-effective variation on the traditional objective structured clinical experience" in which learners move in groups through stations, one member leading the interaction with a standardized participant while others observe. This implementation was a virtual, 2-h course with a 30-min orientation, three 20-min stations with SPs, and a 25-min group debrief, followed by a handout on recruitment best practices. SPs completed an "11-item communication checklist evaluating the learner on a series of established behaviorally anchored communication skills" during debriefs. The concrete-experience-then-reflective-observation model follows Kolb's experiential learning theory.
requirements: Standardized participants (or role-play substitutes) trained on case portrayal and checklist completion
Faculty observers who provide immediate feedback and lead debriefs
A virtual conferencing platform for remote delivery
constraints: Internet connectivity challenges limited checklist completion at the first session
Delivered via a remote (zoom) platform due to the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: research staff who recruit older adults to clinical trials
staff involved in recruitment training and strategy
target_learning_goals: building trust and rapport with participants
assessing understanding and capacity to consent
examples: Three cases: a Black woman with hearing impairment, a white woman and her family member with differing views on research participation, and a Black man with concerns given a history of racism in medical research; conducted five times with 9 participants each.

title: Google Forms for real-time scoring of student answers
description: Google Forms is a free tool the authors use to collect students' answers in class. constraints: The article describes it as supporting answer collection and immediate feedback, not as a replacement for formal assessment formats
examples: The authors report actively using Google Forms to collect students' answers during class, with automatic real-time scoring and pre-entered explanations
